source: Jaensch and Birkhofer (2006) The development of the guideline VDI 2221 - the change of direction
finding: VDI 2221 grew from a line of guidelines: Kesselring 1954 (own inventions), Hansen 1965 (stepped system), VDI 2222 (1973), VDI 2221 (1993). Each step moved from advice on thinking toward abstract process steps.
numbers: Kesselring list has 10 items; VDI 2222 Weissdruck is 52 pages; VDI 2221 Weissdruck is 42 pages, about one third on CAD and data processing. VDI 2222 has 4 phases; VDI 2221 has 7 stages and 4 phases.
limits: Historical account by two insiders of the VDI committee tradition. No outcome data.
agent_relevance: The schema's staged flow (S1 clarify, S2 decompose) has a long lineage, but the lineage is mostly authority, not tested effect.

source: Jaensch and Birkhofer (2006) The development of the guideline VDI 2221 - the change of direction
finding: VDI 2221 dropped the thinking advice and the decision steps that VDI 2222 had. The guideline became more abstract and less usable as direct instruction. The authors say this helps explain the reserved uptake by practitioners.
numbers: VDI 2222 flow had decisions at each step (go on or repeat earlier steps). VDI 2221 figure shows only instructions and results. Checking questions and advice on thinking failures were removed.
quote: The advice within the guidelines have changed from addressing concrete thinking processes to general problem solving advice.
limits: Authors interpret; they did not measure uptake.
agent_relevance: Stage lists without per-step checks are weak. Our states carry explicit pass/fail checks (G2, G3), which VDI 2221 removed.

source: Jaensch and Birkhofer (2006) The development of the guideline VDI 2221 - the change of direction
finding: VDI 2221 stages: clarify task; determine functions and structure; search solution principles and combinations; divide into realisable modules; develop layout of key modules; complete overall layout; prepare production and operating instructions. Each stage yields a named result.
numbers: Results by stage: specification, function structures, principal solutions, module structures, preliminary layouts, definitive layouts, product documents. Iteration is allowed backwards and forwards; the requirements list is adapted throughout.
limits: Describes the 1993 version. The 2019 revision (VDI 2221-1) was not read.
agent_relevance: Concrete model for S1 (clarify and write a requirements list) and S2 (function structure, solution principles). Each stage ends in a checkable artifact.

source: Jaensch and Birkhofer (2006) The development of the guideline VDI 2221 - the change of direction
finding: VDI 2222 advised starting with abstraction of the task to free the designer from fixation on a solution.
numbers: Quote from the Weissdruck of VDI 2222 (1973).
quote: To free oneself of fixation on solutions, it is advisable to start with the abstraction of the task
limits: Advice only; no test in this paper.
agent_relevance: Matches the abstraction step in S1: restate the problem solution-neutrally before generating attempts.

source: Motte (2015) Effectiveness of the systematic engineering design methodology (ICED15)
finding: Review of published tests of the whole systematic method. Verdict: cannot conclude it is ineffective; cannot conclude it beats an intuitive approach. Designer experience and motivation matter at least as much as method.
numbers: More than 30 documented industrial applications (1971-2014), all reported successful. Source screened ICED from 1981, Design conferences from 2002, Konstruktion journal from 1981.
quote: there is neither much evidence that the systematic methodology is significantly more effective than a designer not using it
limits: Review by one author; screening limited to those venues; only whole-method or whole-phase studies kept.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a staged scaffold wins by default. G7 (must pay for itself) is the right stance.

source: Motte (2015) Effectiveness of the systematic engineering design methodology (ICED15)
finding: The positive industrial cases are not independent. Almost all were written by proponents, students or colleagues of Pahl, Beitz, Roth, Rodenacker or Wallace, and mostly from the 1970s to 1990s.
numbers: Named links: Collin under Rodenacker; Schmidt and Hoehn under Beitz; Derhake PhD under Roth; Hales under Wallace. Table 1 lists about 30 cases.
limits: Selection and allegiance bias; no matched control without method in these cases.
agent_relevance: Treat success stories of staged methods as weak evidence. Prefer controlled comparisons.

source: Pahl (1990) lever exercise, as reported in Motte (2015)
finding: About 540 designers in 21 seminars designed a cast lever. 90% drew solution b1 at once. After teaching abstraction, solution principles and selection, final solutions cost 43% and 31% of the material cost of the original.
numbers: N about 540 designers; 21 seminars; material cost 43% (variant f2) and 31% (variant f3) of the first solution.
limits: Second-hand report. No control group redesigning without the method. The comparison is first intuitive draft vs later redesign, so extra time and a second try are confounded with the method.
agent_relevance: Fits a pattern: abstract, then generate several principles, then select, beats the first draft. A cheap analogue for our attempt, restate, re-attempt loop. But the control is weak.

source: Birkhofer (1991) coordinate table, as reported in Motte (2015)
finding: One product (3D-coordinate table) developed with and without the systematic approach. The systematic version was better, mainly through fewer parts. Birkhofer says success cannot be credited to method alone. In two variant-design examples the method helped much less than in new design.
numbers: Single case, two conditions (with, without).
limits: N=1 case; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Gain from staged method is larger for new design than for variant design. Expect the same for novel vs routine tasks.

source: Fricke and Pahl (1991); Fricke (1993, 1999), as reported in Motte (2015)
finding: Study of 15 designers. Good design quality went with adequate decomposition, several variants, and proper assessment of them; also with solution-neutral requirements. But those who strictly followed VDI 2221 did worse than flexible ones.
numbers: N=15 engineers. Strict VDI 2221 followers less successful than flexible followers (no effect size given in the review).
limits: Second-hand. Fricke 1993 finding quoted via Bender (2004).
agent_relevance: Supports keeping the content (decompose, vary, assess) while dropping rigid sequencing. This is the case for state transitions chosen by evidence (G1) rather than a fixed ladder.

source: Pahl (1992) and Ehrlenspiel and Dylla (1991), as reported in Motte (2015)
finding: Pahl observed 4 of 21 designers: the two experienced designers got among the best results, the two inexperienced method-trained ones among the worst. The experienced and trained one was best; the experienced intuitive one took half the time. Ehrlenspiel and Dylla saw no effectiveness difference among 6 designers using different strategies.
numbers: N=4 (of 21) in Pahl; N=6 in Ehrlenspiel and Dylla.
limits: Tiny samples; second-hand.
agent_relevance: Method adds most when paired with domain knowledge. A scaffold cannot replace the model's own knowledge.

source: Rueckert, Schroda, Gaedeke (1997, 1998), as reported in Motte (2015)
finding: 16 student groups (79 students) taught Pahl and Beitz did a semester industrial project. No link between how strictly method was followed and design quality in the first report. In the follow-up, flexible-method groups scored best, then no-method groups, and strict followers last.
numbers: 16 groups, 79 students. Order of quality: flexible > none > strict. One flexible group with little field experience failed and needed the strict method first.
quote: One reason proposed was that students needed to concentrate both on the methods and the results
limits: Second-hand; German-language; no test statistics given.
agent_relevance: Strict stage-following had a cost: attention went to the method, not to the product. G7 (setup cost counts) applies. Novices at the task may need the stages.

source: Bender (2004) and Bender and Blessing (2004), as reported in Motte (2015)
finding: Students with or without systematic design education: no difference in conceptual design quality. Only one group (educated plus experienced, n=5, vs controls n=9) was slightly better in embodiment, p=.04 median test. By actual process style, only 8 students followed VDI 2221 top-down and they had the poorest quality.
numbers: Groups: A1 n=47; VG A2 n=9; VG A3 n=5; KG A2 n=13; KG A3 n=9. Four styles: hierarchical phase-oriented (VDI 2221), hierarchical object-oriented, opportunistic-associative, trial and error. VDI-style n=8.
limits: Small cells; one marginal p; second-hand via Motte.
agent_relevance: Strongest controlled-style evidence against rigid stage order. Opportunistic strategies did better in early embodiment.

source: Motte, Bjoernemo, Andersson (2005); Eisentraut (1999), as reported in Motte (2015)
finding: 30 master students: process quality did not predict result quality in embodiment design. Verbal protocols showed some barely systematic and some very systematic students, with no effect on outcome. Eisentraut (15 students): a result-oriented student took half the time of a thorough systematic one and got a better product; the systematic one missed central requirements.
numbers: N=30 reports; N=15 students in Eisentraut; time ratio 1:2.
limits: Second-hand; very small samples.
agent_relevance: A heavy clarification phase can still miss central requirements. A check against the requirement list (G3) matters more than the volume of analysis.

source: Roth (1995) corkscrew, as reported in Motte (2015)
finding: With full function synthesis and a separate search of physical effects, all solution principles (3.2.1.1 to 3.2.2.2) were found. With function synthesis but effects searched together with embodiment, only 3.2.1.1 to 3.2.1.5. The rest would be accidental discoveries.
numbers: One worked example: increase manual force to remove a cork.
limits: Worked example, not an experiment; no human or control sample.
agent_relevance: Evidence that separating abstract function from physical principle widens coverage of the solution space. Suggests an operator that enumerates principles before details.

source: Pahl and Beelich (1981) survey, as reported in Motte (2015)
finding: Survey of 14 companies: a formal process model was generally not followed; practice was opportunistic. Firms that introduced it consistently reported more protective patents, shorter total development time despite a long concept phase, and better solutions.
numbers: 14 companies; self-report; author is Pahl's collaborator.
limits: Self-reported, no control, mixed full and partial use, proponent authorship.
agent_relevance: Weak support for time savings from a long concept phase. Test on our agent rather than trust.

source: Jensen and Andreasen (2010) Design methods in practice - beyond the systematic approach of Pahl and Beitz
finding: Ethnomethodological critique: Pahl and Beitz treat a method as a road to follow. In practice firms skip, reorder and reinterpret steps. Student case studies in Danish firms found anomalies in objects, steps and goals.
numbers: About 50 master students per year over 3 years. Example: in a 12-step branding method the full sequence was the exception; one firm had about 30% of projects arising outside its formal technology planning.
quote: It seems that the description of method use as taking one prescribed step after another is grossly inaccurate.
limits: Qualitative; not a test of design quality; Danish firms; course authors teach the critique.
agent_relevance: The method is a resource used with judgment, not an algorithm. The program (not the model) should decide transitions, using state evidence.

source: Jensen and Andreasen (2010)
finding: Pahl and Beitz themselves allow slack: if a flash of insight gives the best solution fast, no need to follow all steps; but they say this seldom happens, especially when learning.
numbers: Quote from the Student Edition foreword, 1988.
limits: A statement of intent, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Matches G6/G1: take a fast good answer when checks pass; use stages when they fail.

source: Kannengiesser and Gero (2017) Can Pahl and Beitz' systematic approach be a predictive model of designing? Design Science 3:e24
finding: Coded the 4 phases into the Function-Behaviour-Structure schema: 87 elementary steps (235 with assumed iteration: task clarification and detail once, conceptual and embodiment twice). Compared with student protocols.
numbers: Study 1: 15 two-student sessions, 45 min, second-year mechanical engineering. Study 2: 31 sessions: brainstorming 10, morphological analysis 11, TRIZ 10. Linearity cut-off R2 >= 0.95; 85% aggregation threshold.
quote: The results indicate that the Systematic Approach can predict some but not all of students' design issue behaviour.
limits: Students from one university; occurrences and iteration counts assumed; cross-phase iteration not modelled; tests the process shape only, not design quality.
agent_relevance: A computable form of the staged model exists (FBS issue sequence). Could be used to log what our agent actually does against S1 to S3.

source: Kannengiesser and Gero (2017)
finding: Students matched the prediction for early-versus-late focus on requirements, function and expected behaviour. They did NOT match on structure: students worked on structure and structure-behaviour from the start, which the model puts later. Requirements and description linearity also differed in Study 1.
numbers: Structure slope similar between model and students; structure-behaviour slope differed a lot in Study 2 (much lower in the model). Requirements had under 10 occurrences in Study 2, so no result.
limits: Exact slope values were in tables not in the text I read. Authors blame skipped task clarification or overlapping phases.
agent_relevance: Natural designers (and likely LLMs) jump to concrete structure early. A scaffold must force abstract steps on purpose; they will not occur by default.

source: Fiorineschi, Frillici, Rotini (2018) Supporting systematic conceptual design with TRIZ (Design 2018)
finding: Systematic conceptual design rests on functional decomposition and morphology (FDM, Pahl et al. 2007). A known flaw is weak support for innovative solutions. Attempts to bolt TRIZ on face clashes in how function is defined.
numbers: Cites Ullman (2010): early decisions affect about 80% of product cost. The paper gives three academic application examples, not a controlled test.
limits: Conceptual proposal; no controlled data on creativity gain.
agent_relevance: FDM gives coverage, not novelty. Novelty needs a separate operator judged by running (G8).

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2023) Conceptual design generation using large language models (IDETC; arXiv:2306.01779)
finding: GPT-3 generated 100 solutions for each of 12 design problems; compared with crowdsourced human solutions. Experts rated LLM solutions higher on feasibility and usefulness, crowd higher on novelty. Not a staged-method test, but the baseline for single-shot LLM concept generation.
numbers: 12 problems; 600 solutions rated (20 per problem and mode, 120 per condition pair) by 2 trained experts on 0-2 scales; mean nearest-sample cosine similarity few-shot 0.804 (SD 0.06), zero-shot with 'unique' 0.746 (SD 0.06). Model repeats itself after a few solutions.
limits: Old model (GPT-3); two raters; kappa only fair to moderate; text embeddings for diversity.
agent_relevance: A plain model gives feasible but unoriginal ideas and repeats. Staging alone does not fix repetition; diversity needs a code check (G4, G5).

source: Chen et al. (2024) Towards controllable generative design: FBS ontology and large language models. J Mech Des 146(12), doi:10.1115/1.4065562
finding: Closest LLM test of a Pahl-and-Beitz-like requirement -> function -> behaviour -> structure chain. ChatGPT was prompted by three fixed templates ('What functions should a X have?', 'What kind of design can afford F?', 'What design structures can achieve B?'). 80 designers sketched a leg rehabilitation device from the output.
numbers: 80 designers (60 novices, 20 professionals), 20 per group, 30 min. Mean concept score vs a Red Dot reference scored 3 on 5 criteria: FBS group 3.31 (SD 0.58), fixed-prompt group 2.94 (0.55), free ChatGPT 2.90 (0.47), search engine only 2.63 (0.53). ANOVA F about 15.99, p 1.7e-9. t-tests: FBS vs free p=4.8e-5; FBS vs search p=1e-9. 3 expert raters, Fleiss kappa 0.66.
limits: One task; sketching adds noise; user picks which function words to keep (human in the loop); t-tests appear to treat criteria scores as independent samples, which probably overstates significance; baseline is the human with ChatGPT, not the model alone.
agent_relevance: Evidence that staged decomposition prompts raise concept quality over free prompting (3.31 vs 2.90). Gains in feasibility and usability. The selecting step was a human; our program must do it with checks.

source: Chen et al. (2024)
finding: Per-criterion pattern: FBS group beat the free-form group most on feasibility, usability, functionality for novices. On novelty, free-form professionals (3.73) and fixed-prompt professionals (3.60) were at or above FBS professionals (3.53).
numbers: Novices: feasibility FBS 3.64 vs free 2.85; usability 3.58 vs 2.49; functionality 3.26 vs 2.40. Professionals: novelty free 3.73, fixed 3.60, FBS 3.53.
limits: Cells of 5 professionals per group; no per-criterion tests reported.
agent_relevance: Staging helps correctness-type qualities more than novelty. Matches Fiorineschi: FDM is weak on creativity.

source: Massoudi and Fuge (2025) Agentic large language models for conceptual systems engineering and design (arXiv:2507.08619v2)
finding: Nine-role multi-agent system (requirements, functional decomposition, simulator code) vs a two-agent Generator-Reflector loop, on a solar water filtration brief. Requirement coverage stayed under 20% for every setting. The staged system did not beat the simple loop on code that runs.
numbers: 60 runs (2 LLMs x 2 systems x 3 temperatures x 5 seeds). Code executability: Llama MAS 40.2/46.8/49%, Llama 2AS 62.9/94.7/5% at T=0/0.5/1; R1 MAS 34.8/1.3/5%, R1 2AS 100/66/4%. Requirements coverage max 20% (R1 MAS T=0). JSON validity and embodiment tag 100%. Only R1 completed the workflow (MAS 2,3,2 of 5 seeds; 2AS 5,3,0). MAS graph nodes 5-6 with R1; 2AS mode-collapsed.
limits: 70B open models; one case; small seeds; no human quality rating; the role pipeline is not Pahl and Beitz exactly.
agent_relevance: A bigger staged pipeline gave more detail but worse runnable output than a two-agent loop at several settings. Stages cost tokens and can lose requirements. Supports G7: test every stage at equal tokens.

source: Bhattacharya, Majumder, Chakrabarti (2024) Effect of reference knowledge choice in generating SAPPhIRE content using an LLM (arXiv:2407.00396)
finding: An LLM was used to fill a causal function-model (SAPPhIRE) with retrieval. Authors report that choice of reference knowledge strongly affects the accuracy of the generated technical content.
numbers: Abstract-level finding read; detailed accuracy numbers not extracted this session.
limits: Only abstract and introduction read. Part one of a two-part study.
agent_relevance: Function-model slots filled by an LLM need grounded sources. Hallucination risk in S2 function structures; check against references.

source: Jiang, Li, Qian, Zhang, Luo (2025) AutoTRIZ (arXiv:2403.13002v4)
finding: LLM pipeline that runs the TRIZ steps (contradiction, principles, solution report). On 10 textbook cases, the top-3 detected contradictions matched or half-matched the textbook in 7 cases.
numbers: 7 of 10 cases match or half-match in top 3; entropy of detections is higher where agreement is lower; higher-probability outputs matched better. Battery thermal management case study reports +24% / +64% / +26% on three metrics vs best existing scheme.
limits: Textbook answers are not a gold standard (authors say so); only 10 cases; the case study is the authors' own design.
agent_relevance: Self-consistency across runs signals reliability of a structured step: agreement as a hint (G4), not proof.

source: Marini and Krus (2026) Context operations to architecture modelling output from LLMs (arXiv:2609.10132)
finding: Framework for assembling modular context units (policy prompts, persistent reference units, user questions) and a method to evaluate modelling-as-code output for compliance to intent.
numbers: Framework paper; I found no Pahl-and-Beitz comparison or accuracy table in the parts read.
limits: Opened and skimmed only; not a test of a staged design method.
agent_relevance: Low direct relevance. Notes that structured context assembly is being formalised for engineering design.

source: Search note (this run)
finding: Searches found no LLM paper that runs the full Pahl and Beitz or VDI 2221 sequence and measures it against a plain model. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv APIs were rate-limited, so absence is not proven.
numbers: Web searches: 6 used. Closest are Chen 2024 (FBS chain) and Massoudi 2025 (multi-agent early design).
limits: Gap may be a search artifact. Chen et al. DRS 2024 LLM-augmented morphological analysis (doi 10.21606/drs.2024.605) was seen only as an abstract: three stages (decompose, generate, combine); claims better quality and lower cognitive load; no numbers read.
agent_relevance: Open question for the schema: no direct published test of a full staged-design scaffold for LLMs. Our own measurement would be the evidence (G7).
